nameStory: Small bur-reed gets its name from its spiky, round seed heads that look like tiny medieval maces or burrs that might stick to your clothing. The 'small' part distinguishes it from its much larger cousins - this is the petite member of the bur-reed family. Like many water plants, it was named for the most obvious feature you'd notice: those distinctive bristly spheres floating on the water's surface.
description: Small bur-reed is a delicate aquatic plant that spends most of its life floating just beneath or at the water's surface in quiet ponds and slow streams. It looks like thin, ribbon-like grass floating in the water, with narrow green leaves that bend and sway with the current. The plant produces distinctive round, spiky flower and seed heads that look like tiny green pin cushions bobbing on the water. It's much smaller and more delicate than other bur-reeds you might encounter.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Two types of round, ball-shaped flower heads - white fluffy male flowers that look like tiny cotton balls, and green female flowers covered in short, pointed spikes like a miniature medieval mace

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thin, grass-like leaves that feel soft and flexible when floating in water, but become tougher and shorter when the plant is stranded at the waterline during low water periods

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Usually completely submerged or floating at the water surface in calm, shallow areas - rarely stands upright above water like its larger relatives

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small green or brown seed-like fruits (achenes) arranged in spiky, round clusters that feel prickly to the touch but won't actually hurt you

habitat: Look for small bur-reed in shallow, calm waters like quiet pond edges, slow-moving stream backwaters, and protected coves of larger lakes. It prefers spots where the water barely moves and is usually less than a few feet deep. You'll often find it mixed with other floating aquatic plants in areas with soft, muddy bottoms.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge and begin floating as water temperatures warm, appearing as fresh green ribbons just under the surface.
seasonality.summer: Distinctive round flower heads appear - first the white fluffy male flowers, followed by the spiky green female flowers. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and the spiky seed heads turn brown, while leaves may start to yellow and break apart as water temperatures cool.
seasonality.winter: Most above-water parts die back, leaving the plant dormant in the mud until spring - nearly impossible to identify during this season.

funFact: Small bur-reed is like nature's own mood ring - the same plant can look completely different depending on water levels! When water is high, it develops long, flowing leaves that dance underwater, but when water drops and leaves it high and dry, it transforms into a compact, tough little plant with short, stubby leaves.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other floating grass-like water plants, but those distinctive spiky, round flower and seed heads are a dead giveaway - no other small aquatic plant in New England has flowers that look like tiny medieval weapons floating on the water.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'least' or 'small' bur-reed, this plant has one of the widest distributions in the world, found across North America, Europe, and Asia. However, it's quite rare in New England with only a handful of documented locations, making any sighting special.
compareHints: Small bur-reed is much more delicate and usually stays submerged compared to its relatives like American bur-reed or big bur-reed, which stand tall above water like cattails. While other bur-reeds have sturdy, upright stems and larger flower heads, small bur-reed's flowers are tiny and the whole plant has a delicate, floating habit. Think of it as the shy, floating cousin in a family of bold, upright water plants.

relatedSpecies.distinction: American bur-reed can be distinguished from its bur-reed relatives primarily by size and habitat - it's mid-sized compared to the massive big bur-reed or the tiny small bur-reed.
Big bur-reed stands out from other bur-reeds by being the largest and having the biggest, most impressive spiky seed heads - it's truly the giant of the group.
Floating bur-reed differs from its relatives by truly living up to its name - it floats more readily than American or big bur-reed, which tend to grow in shallower water with more erect stems.
Among New England's bur-reeds, this species has the narrowest leaves and is the most aquatic, rarely growing in anything but deep water.
Among New England's bur-reeds, unbranched bur-reed is distinguished by its single, straight flowering stem and relatively wide leaves with keeled bases.
Branching bur-reed is distinguished from other bur-reeds primarily by its branching flower arrangement - most other species like unbranched bur-reed keep their spiky balls in a simple single row.
